Yes, such a sequence exists. Here is the proof.

**Setup.** Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be non-decreasing. We construct continuous non-decreasing $f_n$ with $\|f_n-f\|_{L^1}\to 0$.

**Step 1. Extension to $\mathbb{R}$.** Define $\tilde f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ by
$$\tilde f(x)=\begin{cases} f(a) & x<a,\\ f(x) & a\le x\le b,\\ f(b) & x>b.\end{cases}$$
This is non-decreasing on $\mathbb{R}$, bounded, and agrees with $f$ on $[a,b]$.

**Step 2. Mollification.** Let $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ be the standard non-negative mollifier with $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq[-1,1]$ and $\int\rho=1$, and set $\rho_n(t)=n\rho(nt)$. Define
$$g_n(x)=(\tilde f * \rho_n)(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\tilde f(x-t)\rho_n(t)\,dt.$$
Each $g_n$ is $C^\infty$, hence continuous.

**Step 3. Monotonicity.** For $x_1<x_2$,
$$g_n(x_2)-g_n(x_1)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl[\tilde f(x_2-t)-\tilde f(x_1-t)\bigr]\rho_n(t)\,dt\ge 0,$$
since $\tilde f$ is non-decreasing and $\rho_n\ge 0$. So $g_n$ is non-decreasing on $\mathbb{R}$.

**Step 4. $L^1$ convergence on $[a,b]$.** Since $\tilde f\in L^1_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R})$, the standard mollification theorem gives $g_n\to\tilde f$ in $L^1_{\text{loc}}(\mathbb{R})$, in particular $\int_a^b|g_n-\tilde f|\to 0$. As $\tilde f=f$ on $[a,b]$,
$$\int_a^b|g_n-f|\,dx\to 0.$$

**Step 5. Restriction.** Set $f_n=g_n\big|_{[a,b]}$. Each $f_n$ is continuous (even smooth) and non-decreasing on $[a,b]$, and $\|f_n-f\|_{L^1([a,b])}\to 0$.

**Conclusion.** The sequence $(f_n)$ satisfies all the required properties, so such a sequence always exists.

### PROOF COMPLETE
